sermon.title: The Last Sermon
sermon.lead: On the ninth of Dhul-Hijjah in the year 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ rode into the valley at Arafah and addressed the largest gathering of his life, more than a hundred thousand pilgrims who had come to learn their Hajj from him. He was sixty-three, about three months from his death, and his words show he sensed it. That same day, while he stood at Arafah, the verse descended: ’This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favor upon you, and approved for you Islam as religion.’ (5:3) What follows is his testament, spoken while the religion itself was being sealed.

sections.h: I May Not Meet You After This Year
sections.body: Jabir ibn Abdullah, who preserved the fullest account of that pilgrimage, describes the Prophet ﷺ riding his camel al-Qaswa into the belly of the valley and calling the people to hear him. Through those days he kept saying: ’Take your rites from me, for I do not know; perhaps I shall not perform Hajj after this Hajj of mine.’ The companions heard the farewell inside the instruction, and the journey itself came to be named Hajjat al-Wada, the Farewell Pilgrimage. So everything said at Arafah carries the weight of a man setting his house in order before the largest audience he would ever have, saying, while there was still time, what must never be forgotten.

sections.h: The Sanctity of Blood, Wealth and Honor
sections.body: He began where every narration of that day begins: ’Indeed your blood and your wealth are sacred to you, as sacred as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours.’ His listeners measured holiness by three things above all: the day of Arafah, the month of Dhul-Hijjah, the precincts of the Haram. He took the most inviolable things they knew and made every believer’s life and property their equal. In the khutbah at Mina days later he ﷺ joined a third term to the pair: ’your blood, your wealth, and your honor.’ Reputation, dignity, the good name of another Muslim, all fenced by the same sanctity. Whoever carries this sermon leaves it knowing that the person beside him is sacred ground.

Then he dismantled the old world: ’Every matter of Jahiliyyah is laid down beneath these two feet of mine.’ The blood feuds of the age of ignorance were cancelled, and he began with his own house: ’The first blood claim I abolish is our own blood, the blood of the son of Rabi’ah ibn al-Harith,’ a child of his kinsman, killed as a nursling among Banu Sa’d. The riba of Jahiliyyah, its usury, was annulled the same way: ’The first riba I abolish is our riba, the riba of Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib; it is cancelled, all of it.’ He demanded of his own family first what he demanded of everyone, and no reform in history has begun closer to home.

’Fear Allah concerning women, for you have taken them by the covenant of Allah, and their companionship has been made lawful to you by the word of Allah.’ In his final public teaching, marriage is a trust sworn in the name of Allah. The duties run both ways: a wife is not to admit into the home anyone her husband dislikes, and ’their right upon you is their provision and their clothing, according to what is honorable.’ The clause permitting, after betrayal of that trust, a discipline ’without severity’ was fenced tightly by the jurists and never once practiced by the Prophet ﷺ, who struck no woman and no servant, ever. Tirmidhi’s farewell narration adds his ﷺ plain command: ’Treat women well.’

The sanctities knit the believers into a single family, and the gravest breach of them is to draw a brother’s blood. During that same pilgrimage he ﷺ told Jarir to call the people to silence, then said: ’Do not return after me to being unbelievers, striking the necks of one another.’ To kill a believer is to fall back into the darkness that had just been placed under his feet. Property follows the same rule: he taught that nothing of a Muslim’s wealth is lawful to another except what is given with a willing soul. And his ﷺ standing definition held the rest together: ’The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, does not forsake him, does not despise him.’

The most quoted line of the famous composite does not come from the Arafah text preserved in Muslim; it comes from a khutbah during the days of Mina, on the same pilgrimage, a few days later: ’O people, your Lord is one, and your father is one. No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab; no red over black, nor black over red, except by taqwa.’ The words are authentically his ﷺ: the narration in Musnad Ahmad carries a chain graded sahih by the hadith editors of our era. It is marked debated here for placement only, because honesty requires saying that this declaration belongs to Mina, not to the Arafah sermon into which the composite stitches it.

sections.h: What He Left Behind: The Book of Allah
sections.body: ’I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah.’ This is the wording preserved in Muslim’s account of Arafah, and it is the sermon’s center of gravity: the community was about to lose its Prophet ﷺ, never its guidance. Two related wordings deserve honest labels. ’The Book of Allah and my Sunnah’ appears in later collections through chains the scholars grade variously; it is not in the sahih Arafah text. And the ’two weighty things,’ the Book of Allah and the Prophet’s ﷺ household, is authentic in Muslim but belongs to Ghadir Khumm, on the road home after the Hajj. At Arafah itself, the anchor he named was the Book.

sections.h: Let the Present Convey to the Absent
sections.body: The sermon was not meant for the valley alone. In the khutbah at Mina he ﷺ commanded: ’Let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent, for perhaps the one present will convey it to someone who retains it better than he.’ One sentence turned a hundred thousand listeners into transmitters, and everything that followed, the memorizers, the written collections, the sciences built to test every link of every chain, unfolds from it. It also quietly includes you. Fourteen centuries of conveying were set in motion so that these words would find the absent, and the absent, that day, meant every Muslim not yet born.

He closed by handing the verdict on his own mission first to his people, then to his Lord. ’You will be asked about me. What will you say?’ They answered: ’We bear witness that you have conveyed, fulfilled, and given sincere counsel.’ Then he raised his forefinger toward the sky and turned it down toward the people, saying: ’O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness,’ three times. A hundred thousand witnesses, and the Witness above them all. Then Bilal called the adhan, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed Zuhr and Asr joined together in the valley, and stood in supplication at Arafah until the sun set. About three months later he returned to his Lord, and the trust he confirmed that day remains conveyed.

sermon.honesty: The text most widely shared online as ’The Last Sermon’ is a composite: several narrations of different dates and different strength, stitched into one smooth speech. Honesty requires saying so plainly. The core is beyond doubt: Sahih Muslim 1218, the long hadith of Jabir, preserves the Arafah khutbah itself, with the sanctity of blood and wealth, the abolition of the blood claims and riba of Jahiliyyah beginning with the Prophet’s ﷺ own family, the rights of and duties toward women, and holding fast to the Book of Allah. Other beloved lines are authentic but were spoken at Mina during the same pilgrimage, above all ’there is no superiority of Arab over non-Arab except by taqwa,’ which comes from a separate authentic narration in Musnad Ahmad, not from the Arafah text. A few flourishes in circulating versions have no strong chain at all. Every section below carries a label, so that what you read here stands exactly as the evidence stands.

soul.title: Death and the Journey of the Soul
soul.lead: There is one journey every reader of this page will make, and it is the one we study least. The Qur’an and the Sunnah study it in detail: what the soul feels as it leaves the body, how the heavens receive it, what is asked in the grave and by whom, what still reaches the dead from the world of the living, and what the long wait is until the Trumpet sounds. None of it was revealed to terrify. It was revealed so that the believer travels a road already mapped, toward a Lord already known, and so that grief, when it comes, has somewhere true to stand.

sections.body: Nothing on this road happens early, and nothing happens late. ’Never will Allah delay a soul when its term has come.’ (63:11) ’It is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah, at a term appointed in writing.’ (3:145) The fixed term, the ajal, is among the most consoling doctrines given to the grieving: no accident, no illness, no delayed ambulance, no missed diagnosis took your beloved one hour before the writing. It also quiets the living: guarding your life is commanded, but dread adds nothing to a term already set. ’Say: indeed the death from which you flee will surely meet you.’ (62:8) The question the Qur’an leaves open is never whether, only in what state you will be met.

The long hadith of al-Bara ibn Azib, recorded in Musnad Ahmad and Abu Dawud and graded sahih by many scholars of hadith, is the fullest single map of the crossing. Angels with faces like the sun descend and sit before the dying believer, bringing a shroud and perfume from Paradise. The Angel of Death says: ’O good soul, come out to forgiveness from Allah and His pleasure.’ And the soul flows out ’as a drop flows from the mouth of a waterskin.’ For the one who spent life denying his Lord, the same moment reverses: ’O foul soul, come out to the displeasure and anger of Allah,’ and it is dragged out ’as a skewer is drawn through wet wool.’ Death is one event; dying is two experiences.

The same narration follows the soul upward. Wrapped in its shroud of Paradise, the believer’s soul gives off ’the finest musk found on the face of the earth,’ and every company of angels it passes asks: ’Who is this good soul?’ They answer with the most beautiful of the names he was called in the world, and the gate of each heaven opens, and the angels nearest to Allah in every heaven escort him to the next, up to the seventh, where the command is given: ’Write My servant’s record in Illiyyin,’ and the soul is returned to the body for the questioning. The other soul rises with a stench, is announced by its ugliest names, and for it, as the Qur’an had already said, ’the gates of heaven will not be opened.’ (7:40)

That the dead are questioned is not folklore; it is affirmed in hadith across the collections at a combined strength scholars have described as mutawatir in meaning. Anas reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that when a servant is laid in his grave and his companions turn away, ’he hears the tapping of their sandals,’ and two angels sit him up and ask what he used to say about this man, Muhammad ﷺ. The believer answers: I bear witness that he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger. The Prophet ﷺ taught that this is the meaning of the verse: ’Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word, in this life and in the hereafter.’ (14:27) The angels’ names, Munkar and Nakir, appear in a narration Tirmidhi called hasan gharib. What is tested is not scholarship but allegiance.

Tirmidhi transmits the famous sentence: ’The grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fire.’ Grading honesty: Tirmidhi himself marked the narration gharib, a solitary report, and many later critics judged its chain weak. But its meaning rests on ground that is sound beyond dispute. In al-Bara’s hadith, the believer who answers well is spread bedding from Paradise, a door to Paradise is opened so that its breeze and fragrance reach him, and his grave is widened as far as his eye can see; the other has a door opened onto the Fire, and his grave presses in until his ribs interlock. The sentence in Tirmidhi, whatever its chain, is an honest caption for what the sahih narrations describe.

Between death and the Trumpet lies a third state with a Qur’anic name. ’And behind them is a barzakh, a barrier, until the day they are raised.’ (23:100) A barzakh is an isthmus, a strip between two seas that belongs fully to neither shore. The dead are neither extinguished nor yet judged; they are held, in ease or in distress, in a mode of being the living cannot inspect. Twice the Qur’an lifts the curtain. The family of Pharaoh ’are exposed to the Fire morning and evening’ now, before the Hour is even established. (40:46) And the believer of Surah Ya-Sin is told ’Enter Paradise’ and immediately wishes his people knew what his Lord had forgiven him. (36:26-27) The story, in other words, does not pause at the grave.

Death ends a person’s earning; it does not end their receiving. ’When the human being dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: an ongoing charity, or knowledge that continues to benefit, or a righteous child who prays for him.’ The well you dug goes on watering. The du’a of a child reaches a parent by name. The living can also send gifts across the barrier: when a man told the Prophet ﷺ that his mother had died suddenly, he ﷺ confirmed that charity given on her behalf would benefit her. And when a burial was finished he would stand and say: ’Ask forgiveness for your brother, and ask steadiness for him, for he is being questioned now.’ For the grieving, this is the door left open: you cannot hold them, but you can still give to them, tonight.

The Prophet ﷺ visited his mother’s grave and wept, and those with him wept. ’I asked my Lord for permission to seek forgiveness for her, and it was not granted; and I asked permission to visit her grave, and it was granted. So visit the graves, for they remind you of death.’ Visiting is sunnah, and not for the living only: he taught those who enter a graveyard to speak to its people directly, ’Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings, believers and Muslims. We, if Allah wills, will be joining you.’ The living owe the dead their washing, shrouding, the funeral prayer and burial, debts settled, promises kept, and mention without malice. And they owe them truthfulness about grief: he ﷺ wept, and never called weeping a lack of faith.

The waiting ends with a sound. ’The Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall down stunned, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown a second time, and at once they are standing, looking on.’ (39:68) Surah Ya-Sin lets us hear the risen themselves: ’They will say: woe to us, who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Most Merciful promised; the messengers told the truth.’ (36:51-52) They call the grave a resting place, a marqad; commentators noted that beside what has now begun, even the grave’s long night seems no more than a sleep. Scattered dust is no obstacle to the second creation: ’As We began the first creation, We will repeat it.’ (21:104)

The road’s end is not a place but a seeing. ’Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.’ (75:22-23) On a full-moon night the Prophet ﷺ told his companions: ’You will see your Lord as you see this moon; you will not be crowded in seeing Him.’ One nuance belongs here. Aisha held that the Prophet ﷺ did not see his Lord with his eyes in this world on the night journey, while Ibn Abbas affirmed a seeing, with the heart in one narration; their disagreement concerns this world only. That the believers will see their Lord in the hereafter is agreed upon among Ahl al-Sunnah, and in the hadith of Suhayb nothing given in Paradise is more beloved than that look. For the grieving: this is where the believer’s road was leading.

The Prophet ﷺ said: ’Remember often the destroyer of pleasures,’ meaning death. Tirmidhi carried it and graded it hasan. Often, he said; not always. The sunnah is a remembrance that sweetens the ordinary and unclenches the hand, not a dread that poisons living. His prescriptions are concrete. Keep the will written: a Muslim with anything to bequeath should not let two nights pass without it recorded beside him. Settle debts. Mend severed ties. Keep deeds small and steady, for the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most constant, even if few. He forbade wishing for death, even in suffering. And three days before his own passing he ﷺ set the compass for every dying believer: ’Let none of you die except thinking the best of Allah.’ Hope is not the reward of preparation. It is the method.
